sec.title: Background and Aim
sec.p: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in Alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) has shown therapeutic potential, with variable efficacy and unclear mechanism. Because dietary protein influences gut microbiota composition, we hypothesized that donor dietary preconditioning could enhance FMT efficacy. We therefore examined in a murine ALD model if high-protein donor diet improves FMT outcome.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: ALD was induced in C57BL/6N mice using a Lieber-DeCarli ethanol diet combined with thioacetamide administration for 12 weeks. FMT was performed using stool from diet-modulated donors, and recovery was assessed on day7 post-FMT. Multi-omics analysis using 16s rRNA and mass spectroscopy was performed for Gut microbiota composition, plasma- and stool-metabolome, and hepatic proteomes. Multi-omics outcomes were validated in ALD animal and Huh7 hepatocytes.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Both protein-based FMTs improved ALD recovery; Veg-FMT indicated superior efficacy, significantly reducing hepatic injury (AST 1.2FC, p=0.002; bilirubin 1.2FC, p=0.03; steatosis 1.7FC,p=0.01) and restoring gut barrier integrity (occludin 1.5FC,p=0.04; mucin 2 2.2FC, p=002; and plasma endotoxin 1.7FC, p=0.02). A significant 2FC increase was observed in Lachnospiraceae NK4A136, Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002, and short-chain fatty acids, particularly caproic acid. Functional validation confirmed that caproic acid promoted hepatic fatty acid β-oxidation through PPARα-dependent mechanisms, reducing triglyceride accumulation and lipogenesis in both cellular and animal models.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Donor preconditioning with a plant-protein enriched diet enhances FMT efficacy in ALD by gut microbiota modulation with increased metabolites like caproic acid. These findings highlight a microbiota-metabolite-host axis through which diet-modulated FMT improves hepatic lipid metabolism and injury, and identifies a pathway via which FMT imparts its effect.

abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: This study identifies a mechanistic basis for improving fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) efficacy in alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) by demonstrating that dietary preconditioning of donor microbiota improves therapeutic outcomes. We show that plant protein–modulated donor microbiota supplements abstinence-associated recovery through increased production of the microbial associated metabolite caproic acid, which promotes hepatic fatty acid β-oxidation via PPARα signaling. These findings highlight donor dietary conditioning and microbiota-derived metabolites, rather than microbial composition alone, as important determinants of FMT efficacy. The results suggest that microbial associated metabolites such as caproic acid may represent potential therapeutic targets or biomarkers to enhance and standardize microbiota-based interventions in ALD. Although the current work is based on a murine model, the identified microbiota–metabolite–host metabolic axis provides a framework for future translational studies aimed at optimizing FMT strategies in liver disease.

fn.p: This version of the manuscript has been revised to address the reviewers' comments and includes additional experimental validation, revised analyses, and more cautious interpretation of the mechanistic findings. A biolayer interferometry experiment was added to provide direct biophysical evidence for the interaction between caproic acid and the PPARa ligand-binding domain. The Results, Discussion, and Conclusion were revised to distinguish associative, functional, and biophysical evidence and to describe caproic acid as a candidate microbial mediator rather than a definitive mediator. Additional individual-level correlation analyses linking microbiota, caproic acid, and host phenotypes were incorporated. The manuscript was further revised to address the intermediate phenotype of Egg-FMT, limitations of the one-week post-FMT observation period, the choice of egg albumin as an animal-protein comparator, and limitations related to donor-derived metabolite carryover. Terminology, supplementary figure references, and several overstatements were also corrected. Supplementary materials were updated to include the new analyses and BLI data.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Among alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) patients, a majority develop steatosis, with only 10–35% developing hepatitis, of which 8–20% eventually progress to cirrhosis (1). The pathophysiology of ALD is influenced by compositional shifts in intestinal bacteria (2,3). Alcohol intake reduces bacterial diversity and increases the abundance of Proteobacteria and Enterobacteria and decreases the abundance of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, specifically Lactobacillus species, leading to intestinal barrier dysfunction and endotoxemia (3–5).

Restoration of gut microbial homeostasis has therefore emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has indicated beneficial effects in experimental models and clinical studies of alcoholic hepatitis, including improvements in liver injury and survival (5–9). However, responses to FMT remain variable, probably due to the condition of the patient or an inept donor bacterial composition (10). These findings suggest that donor microbiota characteristics may critically influence therapeutic efficacy, highlighting the need to better understand factors that shape donor microbial function.

Diet is one of the strongest determinants of gut microbiota composition and metabolic activity (11,12). Short-term dietary changes can rapidly alter microbial communities and their metabolite production. Although dietary fiber is widely recognized as a major substrate for microbial fermentation, dietary proteins that escape digestion in the small intestine also reach the colon and can serve as substrates for microbial metabolism (13–15). Microbial fermentation of amino acids produces a variety of metabolites capable of modulating host metabolic and inflammatory pathways (16,17).

Despite these associations, the influence of donor dietary conditioning on FMT efficacy in ALD remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated whether preconditioning donor microbiota with diets enriched in vegetable- or egg-derived proteins could enhance FMT-mediated recovery in a murine model of ALD. Using integrated microbiome, metabolomic, and proteomic analyses, we suggest that vegetable protein–modulated microbiota significantly improve recovery from ALD. This effect is associated with enrichment of short-chain fatty acid producing bacteria and increased production of caproic acid, a microbial associated metabolite that activates hepatic PPARα signaling to enhance fatty acid β-oxidation and reduce hepatic lipid accumulation. These findings highlight dietary modulation of donor microbiota as a potential strategy to improve microbiota-based therapies in alcohol-related liver disease.

sec.title: Protein-conditioned FMT enhances recovery from alcohol-induced liver injury
sec.p: To determine whether donor dietary conditioning improves the therapeutic efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), donor mice were preconditioned with either standard diet, vegetable protein diet, or egg protein diet prior to microbiota transfer (Fig. 1A). FMT was administered to ALD mice following abstinence, and liver injury parameters were assessed seven days after transplantation.

caption.title: Protein-conditioned FMT improves liver function.

(B) Overall, FMT reduced serum AST, ALT and bilirubin levels, with an enhanced reduction in Veg-FMT (all p<0.001). (C) Representative micrographs of liver histology by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson’s trichome (MT) staining and immunohistochemistry for smooth muscle actin protein (α-sma) showing decreased hepatic steatosis (p<0.001) and fibrosis-associated staining (MT and α-sma positive area, p=0.01in both) in protein-conditioned FMT with statistical analysis. (D) Compared with egg-FMT, Veg-FMT led to greater reductions in hepatic Il6 (p=0.04), Tnfα (p=0.06), Tlr4 (p=0.05), (E) Acta2 (p=0.001) and Tgfβ(p<0.001) and increased IL10 (0.02) mRNA expression. (F) Hepatic TGs were significantly reduced in protein-conditioned FMT (Veg-FMT: 1.74FC, p<0.001; Egg-FMT: 1.47FC,p=0.009). The data are presented as the means ± SEMs (standard error of the mean). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 represent intergroup statistics; #p < 0.05, ##p < 0.01, ###p < 0.001 represent the ALD group (one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test).

sec.p: Abstinence alone resulted in partial recovery from liver injury, as indicated by increased food intake (fold change >2, p<0.05) and a reduction in the liver-to-body weight ratio compared with ALD mice (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 1B-C). Serum biochemical analysis confirmed successful induction of liver injury in ALD mice, with significantly elevated levels of AST, ALT, and bilirubin compared with controls. Abstinence significantly reduced these markers relative to ALD mice (Fig. 1B).

FMT further improved liver injury beyond abstinence alone. Standard FMT significantly reduced AST (2.1FC), ALT (2.6FC), and bilirubin (1.8FC) compared with ALD mice (all p<0.001). Protein-conditioned FMT produced greater improvement, with Veg-FMT showing the most pronounced effect. Veg-FMT reduced AST by 2.7FC, ALT by 3.2FC, and bilirubin by 2.6FC compared with ALD mice (all p<0.001) (Fig. 1B).

Histological examination supported these findings. Hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed marked hepatic steatosis and inflammatory infiltration in ALD mice, which were partially improved after abstinence and further ameliorated following FMT treatment (Fig. 1C). Veg-FMT produced the greatest reduction in steatosis, showing an approximately 11FC decrease compared with ALD mice (p<0.001).

Consistent with the histological observations, hepatic triglyceride levels were significantly reduced following protein-modulated FMT. Veg-FMT reduced hepatic triglycerides by 1.74FC (p<0.001), while Egg-FMT reduced triglycerides by 1.47FC (p=0.009) relative to ALD mice (Fig. 1F).

Veg-FMT also significantly improved inflammatory and fibrosis-associated markers. Expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines Il6 (2.54FC reduction, p=0.04), Tnfα (1.29FC reduction, p=0.06), and Tlr4 (1.11FC reduction, p=0.05) decreased following Veg-FMT, while the anti-inflammatory cytokine Il10 increased 1.5FC (p=0.02) (Fig. 1D). Similarly, fibrogenic genes Acta2 (4.1FC reduction, p<0.001) and Tgfβ (3.3FC reduction, p<0.001) were significantly downregulated (Fig. 1E).

Collectively, these findings indicated that dietary conditioning of donor microbiota enhances early recovery from alcohol-induced liver injury, with vegetable protein-modulated microbiota showing the strongest protective effect.

sec.title: Veg-FMT restores intestinal barrier integrity and reduces endotoxemia
sec.p: Chronic alcohol exposure disrupts intestinal barrier integrity, leading to increased gut permeability and translocation of microbial products such as endotoxin, which contribute to hepatic inflammation through the gut–liver axis. To determine whether protein-conditioned fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) improves intestinal barrier function, we examined intestinal histology, tight-junction protein expression, antimicrobial peptides, inflammatory markers, and circulating endotoxin levels following treatment.

Histological analysis of intestinal tissues revealed marked epithelial damage and shortening of intestinal villi in ALD mice compared with control animals (Fig. 2A). Although abstinence resulted in partial recovery of intestinal morphology, FMT treatment further improved epithelial structure. Notably, Veg-FMT restored villus architecture to near-normal morphology, whereas Egg-FMT and standard FMT showed only moderate improvement (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 2A). Consistent with these histological findings, ALD mice exhibited significantly reduced expression of key tight-junction proteins, indicating impaired intestinal barrier function. Veg-FMT significantly increased mRNA expression of Zo-1 (2.04FC, p = 0.05), Occludin (2.31FC, p = 0.03), and Claudin-3 (1.63FC, p = 0.01), and significantly increased ZO-1 protein expression compared with ALD mice (Fig. 2A). These results suggest that Veg-FMT effectively restores epithelial tight-junction integrity disrupted by alcohol exposure.

sec.p: In addition to structural barrier proteins, alcohol exposure also induced intestinal inflammatory responses. Veg-FMT significantly reduced expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines Il6 (4.2FC decrease, p = 0.002), Tnfα (5.6FC decrease, p < 0.001), and Tlr4 (2FC decrease, p = 0.04) compared with ALD mice, while the anti-inflammatory cytokine Il10 increased 2.8FC (p < 0.001) (Additional file 1, S.Fig. 2B). These findings indicated that Veg-FMT attenuates alcohol-induced intestinal inflammation.

Intestinal antimicrobial defense mechanisms were also affected. Expression of the antimicrobial peptides Reg3β (1.98FC increase, p = 0.01) and Reg3γ (2.04FC increase, p = 0.02) was significantly elevated following Veg-FMT compared with ALD mice (Fig. 2C). Alcohol consumption degrades Muc2 in the gut mucus lining, contributing to a leaky gut and elevated endotoxemia (18). Veg-FMT also significantly increased expression of the mucin gene Muc2 expression (1.4FC, p=0.05; Fig. 2D), with a concomitant reduction in plasma endotoxin levels (1.7FC, p=0.02; Fig. 3E). A significant negative correlation was observed between Muc2 and plasma endotoxin levels (Spearman’s ρ= -0.86, p<0.001; Fig. 2F). These findings indicated that Veg-FMT enhances abstinence-associated restoration of intestinal barrier integrity, leading to reduced gut inflammation and endotoxemia.

sec.p: Given the marked restoration of intestinal barrier integrity following Veg-FMT, we next investigated whether these effects were associated with alterations in gut microbial composition.

sec.title: Veg-FMT reshapes gut microbial composition associated with improved metabolic function
sec.p: Given the significant restoration of intestinal barrier integrity following Veg-FMT, we next investigated whether these improvements were associated with changes in gut microbial composition. To address this, 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed on fecal samples from six biological animals per experimental group after FMT treatment.

Analysis of alpha diversity using the Shannon index showed no significant differences in overall microbial diversity among the experimental groups (Additional file 1, S.Fig. 3A). However, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray-Curtis distances revealed clear separation between treatment groups, indicating significant differences in microbial community composition (PERMANOVA p = 0.001). The first two principal coordinates explained approximately 77% of the total variance in microbial composition (Fig. 3A).

Taxonomic profiling revealed that Veg-FMT selectively enriched several bacterial taxa associated with beneficial metabolic functions. In particular, the relative abundance of Akkermansia, Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Parasutterella increased following Veg-FMT treatment compared with ALD mice (Fig. 3B). Differential abundance analysis (FC>2, p<0.05) further identified several taxa significantly altered after Veg-FMT (Additional file 1, Fig. S. 3B, C, D, E and Additional file 2, S-table 2A). The abundances of Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002 (4.1FC, p=0.007), Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 (2.25FC, p=0.02) (SCFA producers that maintain gut barrier function (19)) and Tuzzerella (2.45FC, p=0.006; role in lipid metabolism) exclusively increased post-Veg-FMT (Fig. 3C). The opportunistic taxa Sporosarcina and Vagococcus were exclusively decreased (1.12E-01 FC and 1.11E-02 FC, p<0.001, respectively) suggesting suppression of potentially pathogenic bacterial population. Analysis of taxa shared across treatment groups revealed enrichment of beneficial genera including Aerococcus, Blautia, and Lactobacillus in protein-modulated FMT recipients.

To further investigate the relationship between microbial changes and host physiology, correlation analysis (r2 > 0.7, p<0.05) was performed between differentially abundant bacterial taxa and liver injury parameters (Fig. 3E). Several bacterial taxa enriched after Veg-FMT displayed strong negative correlations with liver injury markers, including serum ALT, AST, bilirubin, and TNFα levels. Notably, Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Tuzzerella showed significant negative correlations with these markers while positively correlating with the intestinal mucus marker Muc2. Together, these findings indicated that Veg-FMT promotes enrichment of beneficial microbial taxa associated with improved intestinal barrier integrity and reduced liver injury. To further explore the potential functional implications of the observed microbial compositional changes, PICRUSt2-based functional inference was performed (Fig. 3D; Additional file 1, Fig. S. F and Additional file 2, S-table 2B). Compared with ALD, Veg-FMT showed significant enrichment of pathways related to amino acid degradation and fatty acid metabolism, including L-leucine degradation (log2FC = 4.74, p = 0.0017), L-tyrosine degradation (log2FC = 4.64, p = 0.0023), octane oxidation (log2FC = 4.86, p = 0.0013), and fatty acid salvage (log2FC = 2.71, p = 0.018). Additional enrichment of lipid biosynthesis pathways such as stearate biosynthesis II (log2FC = 2.09, p = 0.018) and oleate biosynthesis IV (log2FC = 2.01, p = 0.020) further indicated increased microbial fatty-acid metabolic potential. In contrast, several pathways associated with bacterial structural metabolism and carbohydrate degradation, including peptidoglycan biosynthesis II (log2FC = −6.46, p = 0.00023), teichoic acid biosynthesis (log2FC = −5.72, p = 0.0024), and lactose and galactose degradation I (log2FC = −6.74, p = 0.00064), were reduced in Veg-FMT compared with ALD. Collectively, these findings suggest that Veg-FMT is associated with increased predicted microbial metabolic potential, particularly in pathways related to amino acid degradation and fatty acid metabolism.

sec.title: Veg-FMT promotes hepatic metabolic reprogramming through PPARα signaling and fatty acid β-oxidation
sec.p: To determine whether microbiota remodeling induced by Veg-FMT influences hepatic metabolic pathways, we performed quantitative proteomic analysis of liver tissues from control, ALD, and FMT-treated mice.

A total of 3,841 proteins were identified, and unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed clear segregation between treatment groups, indicating substantial remodeling of hepatic protein expression following FMT (Fig. 4A). Pathway enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs; FC > 2, p < 0.05) identified several KEGG pathways associated with metabolic regulation and cellular stress responses (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 4A-E and Additional file 2, S-table 3). The apoptosis pathway, which was elevated in ALD mice, was reversed by all FMT treatments (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 4C-4E). Notably, Veg-FMT uniquely and significantly reduced unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis (p = 0.04) and showed a marginal reduction in the reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathway (p = 0.08; Additional file 1, S. Fig. 4E).

(B) Venn diagram showing the number of common and unique enriched pathways among abst, Std-FMT, Veg-FMT and egg-FMT, with the (C) table showing pathway names. (D) The PPAR signaling pathway was significantly enriched (p=8.3x10-06) in the Veg-FMT group. (E) Hepatic PPARα mRNA expression was greater in the Veg-FMT group (p<0.001) than in the Egg-FMT group. (F) mRNA expression (top panel; Cpt1 (p=0.003), Fabp1 (p=0.005) and peroxisomal Acox1 (p=0.02)) and protein expression (bottom panel; Cpt1a (p=0.007), Acox1 (p= 0.05), Acadm (p= 0.04) and Fabp1 (p= 0.02)) of PPARα target genes involved in fatty acid beta-oxidation increased after Veg-FMT. The data are presented as the means ± SEMs (standard error of the mean). *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 represent intergroup statistics; #p < 0.05, ##p < 0.01, ###p < 0.001 represent the ALD group (one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test).

sec.p: Comparison of common and unique pathways revealed distinct metabolic effects of dietary protein-modulated FMT (Fig. 4B). Stopping alcohol increased oxidative phosphorylation, whereas all FMT treatments significantly enriched pathways related to PPAR signaling, primary bile acid biosynthesis, and endoplasmic reticulum protein processing. In addition, protein-modulated FMT specifically enhanced pathways associated with cholesterol metabolism, fatty acid degradation, and histidine metabolism (Fig. 4C, Additional file 2, S-table 4).

Among the enriched pathways, PPAR signaling emerged as a prominent metabolic pathway associated with FMT-mediated recovery. Given the well-established role of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptors (PPARs) in regulating hepatic lipid metabolism and steatosis (20,21), we further examined proteins associated with this pathway. Enrichment analysis identified 9 proteins linked to PPAR signaling in Veg-FMT (p = 8.3 × 10 ), 7 proteins in Egg-FMT (p = 1.44 × 10 ), and 5 proteins in Std-FMT (p = 0.001; Fig. 4D). Among these, PPARα expression was significantly increased following Veg-FMT (1.7FC vs ALD, p < 0.001; 1.2FC vs Egg-FMT, p < 0.001) (Fig. 4E), whereas PPARγ expression remained unchanged across treatment groups (Additional file 1, S.Fig. 4F).

To determine whether PPARα activation translated into functional metabolic changes, we examined downstream genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation. Both Veg-FMT and Egg-FMT increased β-oxidation–related gene expression; however, Veg-FMT produced significantly stronger effects. Compared with Egg-FMT, Veg-FMT significantly increased expression of mitochondrial Cpt1 (1.25FC, p = 0.003), Fabp1 (1.25FC, p = 0.005), and peroxisomal Acox1 (1.2FC, p = 0.02; Fig. 4F). Consistent with these findings, protein expression of Cpt1a (1.2FC, p = 0.007), Acox1 (1.1FC, p = 0.05), Acadm (1.1FC, p = 0.04), and Fabp1 (1.1FC, p = 0.02) was significantly increased only in Veg-FMT–treated mice; Fig. 4F). Thus, Egg-FMT also engaged PPARα-associated fatty acid metabolic responses, but the magnitude of these responses was consistently lower than that observed with Veg-FMT. Together, these findings indicated that vegetable protein–modulated FMT more effectively activates hepatic PPARα signaling and downstream fatty acid β-oxidation pathways, indicating enhanced hepatic lipid metabolism following Veg-FMT treatment.

sec.title: Veg-FMT mediated metabolic effects are dependent on PPARα signaling
sec.p: To determine whether the metabolic benefits of Veg-FMT were mediated through PPARα signaling, we pharmacologically inhibited PPARα using the antagonist GW6471 in Veg-FMT–treated ALD mice (Fig. 5A). PPARα inhibition significantly reduced hepatic PPARα mRNA expression (4.5FC decrease, p < 0.001; Fig. 5B) and protein levels (2.3FC decrease, p = 0.01; Fig. 5C) compared with Veg-FMT alone. Consistent with suppression of this pathway, inhibition of PPARα resulted in a significant increase in the liver-to-body weight ratio (3.3FC, p = 0.04; Additional file 1, S.Fig. 5A).

sec.p: Systemic markers of liver injury were also markedly elevated following PPARα inhibition, including serum AST (1.7FC, p = 0.003), ALT (2FC, p = 0.002), and bilirubin (2.5FC, p = 0.04), accompanied by increased hepatic triglyceride accumulation (1.45FC, p = 0.03; Fig. 5D). Histological analysis further revealed persistence of hepatic inflammation, steatosis, and fibrosis in the inhibitor-treated group (Additional file 1, S.Fig. 5C; Fig. 5E), indicating loss of the hepatoprotective effects observed with Veg-FMT alone.

PPARα inhibition also impaired intestinal barrier integrity, as evidenced by villus blunting, reduced ZO-1 protein expression (1.97FC decrease, p < 0.001; Additional file 1, S.Fig. 5D), and significantly elevated plasma endotoxin levels (2.3FC increase, p < 0.001; Fig. 5F). Consistently, expression of canonical PPARα target genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, including Cpt1, Acox1, and Fabp1, was markedly suppressed (5FC, 4.3FC, and 4.7FC decreases, respectively; p < 0.001 for all; Additional file 1, S.Fig. 5E).

Interestingly, inhibition of PPARα did not significantly alter overall gut microbiota composition between groups (PERMANOVA p = 0.644; Additional file 1, S.Fig. 6), suggesting that the loss of protection was primarily due to disruption of host metabolic signaling rather than changes in microbial community structure.

sec.title: Metabolomic profiling identifies caproic acid enrichment following Veg-FMT
sec.p: PPARα has multiple metabolic ligands (22). Untargeted metabolomic profiling was performed on stool and plasma samples to identify microbiota associated metabolites potentially involved in PPARα signaling. A total of 665 metabolites in stool and 522 in plasma were detected. Principal coordinate analysis indicated clear separation between experimental groups, with the first two components explaining ∼60% of the variance in stool metabolites and ∼31% in plasma metabolites (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 7A-B). Differential metabolite analysis revealed multiple metabolites significantly altered in Abst- and FMT-treated animals compared with ALD mice (FC>1.5, p<0.05) (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 7C-D; Additional file 2, S-table 5 for stool and S-table 6 for plasma). Unique significantly upregulated metabolites for both stool and plasma were identified (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 7E-F; Additional file 2, S-table 7 for stool and 8 for plasma). Comparative analysis of protein-modulated FMT groups showed 72 metabolites commonly increased in stool and 7 in plasma, whereas Veg-FMT uniquely increased 61 stool and 23 plasma metabolites. Among these metabolites, two molecules were significantly enriched in both stool and plasma following Veg-FMT: N-butanoyl-homoserine lactone and caproic acid (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 7G and Additional file 2, S-table 9). N-butanoyl-homoserine lactone is a bacterial quorum-sensing molecule involved in microbial communication and biofilm regulation (23). In contrast, caproic acid (hexanoic acid) is a microbial fatty acid metabolite associated with anti-inflammatory effects and host energy metabolism (24). Caproic acid levels were significantly increased in Veg-FMT recipients in both stool (2.5FC, p=0.01) and plasma (3.4FC, p = 0.01), and were higher compared with Egg-FMT animals (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 7H-I). Notably, Egg-FMT also showed an increase in caproic acid, although at lower levels than Veg-FMT, consistent with its intermediate hepatic phenotype.

sec.p: These findings identified caproic acid as a candidate microbiota-derived metabolite potentially linking Veg-FMT induced microbiota remodeling with hepatic metabolic responses.. To further examine the relationship between microbiota-associated metabolites and host responses, we performed an integrated Spearman correlation analysis using matched microbiome, metabolomic, and phenotypic data (Additional file 1, Fig. S8; S. Table 10). Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002 were positively associated with caproic acid abundance (ρ=0.713 and 0.678, respectively; FDR q<0.05). Caproic acid was negatively associated with hepatic triglycerides (ρ= -0.797, q=0.006), AST (ρ= -0.779, q=0.008), bilirubin (ρ =-0.764, q=0.009), IL-6 (ρ= -0.763, q=0.009), and ALT (ρ= -0.615, q=0.043). These findings provide associative support for a microbiota-caproic acid-host metabolic axis and supported the selection of caproic acid for subsequent functional validation, while not establishing causality.

sec.title: Caproic acid mitigates ethanol-induced steatosis by enhancing fatty acid β-oxidation in hepatocytes
sec.p: Because fatty acids can function as PPARα ligands (25), we next examined whether caproic acid could modulate PPARα signaling in hepatocytes. Ethanol-exposed Huh7 cells were treated with caproic acid (CA) in the presence or absence of the PPARα inhibitor GW6471 (Fig. 6A). Based on dose-response experiments, 100 mM ethanol and 900 µM caproic acid were selected for subsequent studies (Additional file 1, S.Fig. 9A).

CA supplementation significantly reduced ethanol-induced inflammatory responses, including IL-6 (5FC, p = 0.002) and TNFα (5.5FC, p = 0.006), while increasing the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 (Fig. 6B). These effects were reversed in the presence of GW6471, indicating that the anti-inflammatory effects of CA are mediated through PPARα signaling.

Consistent with this observation, CA markedly suppressed lipogenic gene expression, including Srebp1c (4FC, p < 0.001) andFasn (4.5FC, p < 0.001), while significantly increasing β-oxidation genes, including PPARα (8FC, p < 0.001), Cpt1a (7.6FC, p = 0.001), and Fabp1 (5.7FC, p = 0.002) (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 9B–C). Oil Red O staining confirmed a marked reduction in lipid accumulation following CA treatment (2FC decrease, p = 0.02), which was reversed by PPARα inhibition (Fig. 6C).

Consistently, intracellular triglyceride levels were significantly reduced after CA supplementation (1.7FC decrease, p = 0.05; Fig. 6D), accompanied by reduced expression of the lipid droplet marker PLIN2 (2.07FC decrease, p = 0.002; Fig. 6E). In contrast, genes involved in lipid export (ApoB and MTTP; Additional file 1, S. Fig. 9D) showed only modest and non-significant changes, suggesting that CA-mediated steatosis reduction primarily results from enhanced fatty acid oxidation rather than increased lipid export.

To functionally assess alterations in cellular fatty acid utilization, a Mito Fuel Flex assay was performed. CA significantly increased oxygen consumption associated with fatty acid oxidation (4.2FC, p < 0.001; Fig. 6F), and this effect was completely abolished by GW6471. In comparison, the known PPARα ligand butyric acid (25) induced only a modest increase in fatty acid oxidation (Additional file 1, S. Fig. 9E). Because the Mito Fuel Flex assay assesses cellular substrate dependency and utilization rather than directly quantifying intracellular β-oxidation flux, these findings were interpreted as functional evidence of altered fatty acid utilization rather than a direct measurement of metabolic flux. To further analyse the binding kinetics between PPARα and Caproic acid, we performed biolayer interferometry using recombinant PPARα ligand-binding domain (PPARα-LBD). Caproic acid showed direct concentration-dependent association curves for the increasing concentrations of CA (31.25–500 µM). Each reaction displayed clean association and dissociation curves in 1X PBS as reaction buffer mimicking cellular milieu. Affinity constant of 46µM±7.6E-21M, strengthens our validation for direct interaction between PPARα and Caproic acid (Additional file 1, Fig. S10A-B). These findings provide complementary biophysical evidence for direct interaction between caproic acid and the PPARα ligand-binding domain. Together, these findings support a role for PPARα signaling in the caproic acid-associated reduction of hepatocellular lipid accumulation and altered fatty acid utilization.

sec.title: In vivo confirmation of caproic acid-mediated hepatoprotection
sec.p: To validate these findings in vivo, ALD model mice were supplemented with caproic acid with or without the PPARα inhibitor (Fig. 7A). CA supplementation significantly reduced the liver-to-body weight ratio compared with ethanol-treated mice (1.5 FC, p<0.001; Additional file 1, S. Fig. 11A), CA supplementation also significantly reduced serum markers of liver injury, including AST (3.4FC, p = 0.02), ALT (5.5FC, p < 0.001), and bilirubin (10FC, p = 0.006), whereas these protective effects were completely abolished in the presence of the inhibitor (Fig. 7B).

Histological and biochemical analyses further indicated significant reductions in hepatic lipid accumulation following CA supplementation. Hepatic triglyceride levels decreased significantly (1.6FC, p = 0.02; Fig. 7C), accompanied by marked reductions in H&E-positive steatotic area (5FC, p < 0.001) and Oil Red O-positive lipid accumulation (4.3FC, p < 0.001). CA supplementation also significantly reduced hepatic fibrosis (5FC, p = 0.007; Fig. 7D), reduced hepatic expression of pro-inflammatory markers (IL6, TNFa, IL1b, NFkB and increased the expression of the anti-inflammatory marker (IL10; Additional file 1, S. Fig. 11B). These protective effects were not observed in mice treated with the PPARα inhibitor.

At the molecular level, CA significantly suppressed lipogenic genes, including Srebp1c (4.4FC), Scd1 (7.3FC), and Fasn (2.3FC; p < 0.001 for all), while simultaneously enhancing expression of PPARα and downstream β-oxidation genes, including Cpt1 (7FC, p = 0.01), Acox1 (4.7FC, p = 0.008), and Fabp1 (4.8FC, p = 0.002) (Fig. 7E-F). These transcriptional changes were attenuated upon PPARα inhibition, while the overall hepatoprotective effects of CA were also diminished, supporting a functional role for PPARα signaling in the response to CA. Collectively, these results suggested that caproic acid supplementation mitigates alcohol-induced liver injury by activating PPARα-mediated fatty acid β-oxidation pathways in vivo.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The current study identifies veg-protein enriched donor diet followed by FMT (veg-FMT) as a therapeutic option for ameliorating alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). We identified caproic acid, a six-carbon fatty acid produced by gut bacteria (26), as a candidate microbial mediator associated with PPARα-dependent regulation of hepatic fatty acid metabolism.. A key finding is the significant role of donor preparation, particularly protein supplementation and the kind of protein in the diet, which enhances the efficacy of FMT. By modulating the donor gut microbiota through plant-based proteins, Veg-FMT accelerated and amplified abstinence related recovery, leading to reduced hepatic inflammation and fibrosis-associated markers and staining..

Veg-FMT also significantly enhanced intestinal barrier integrity with a concomitant reduction in plasma endotoxin levels, highlighting its dual action in mitigating gut epithelium damage and limiting systemic inflammation. These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that microbial interventions restore gut permeability and reduce endotoxemia in ALD models (7,27,28).

Additionally, the upregulation of antimicrobial peptides (Reg3β and Reg3γ) highlights the role of Veg-FMT in strengthening mucosal immunity. These peptides likely contribute to maintaining a healthier gut microbiota composition, which is essential for reducing alcohol-induced endotoxemia (29). These findings suggest that the benefits of Veg-FMT rely on preserving intestinal barrier integrity and mucosal defenses, which is consistent with our earlier work showing that plant protein supplementation improved hepatic stress and barrier function in ALD (30).

Donor management plays a pivotal role in the success of FMT (31). Given that diet directly influences the composition of the gut microbiota (12), numerous studies have highlighted the impact of pre-educating donor microbiota with different dietary regimens on the efficacy of FMT (32–34). Kedia et al. reported that FMT plus an anti-inflammatory diet significantly improved UC outcomes, with deep remission maintained for up to a year through ongoing dietary interventions (35). Similarly, Rinott et al. reported that diet-modulated autologous FMT, especially from green-Mediterranean diet donors, reduced weight regain and improved glycemic control, highlighting the lasting metabolic benefits of diet-driven microbiome modulation (36). In addition, Yang et al. suggested that FMT from methionine-restricted diet donors remodeled the gut microbiota in obese mice, increasing SCFA-producing bacteria, reducing proinflammatory taxa, and improving lipid metabolism and fat browning (33). Together, these findings highlight the importance of donor preparation, especially through tailored diets, to increase the therapeutic potential of FMT.

In addition to broader dietary regimens, specific dietary macronutrients, such as proteins, further influence the composition of the gut microbiota (11). While dietary fiber and prebiotic oligosaccharides are established substrates for gut fermentation, emerging evidence shows that small amounts of nondigestible dietary proteins and peptides also reach the colon for microbial metabolism. The differing digestibility of plant- and animal-based proteins shapes their distinct effects on the gut microbiota, with plant proteins, due to lower digestibility and complexity, being more likely to reach the colon and drive unique microbial profiles (37). Egg albumin was selected as the animal-derived protein source because of its well-characterized composition, high biological value, and prior use in our ALD dietary intervention studies (30). However, egg albumin represents only one animal protein source, and other proteins such as casein or whey may produce distinct microbial and metabolic responses. Therefore, our findings should not be generalized to animal proteins as a whole.

In this context, Veg-FMT, which involves plant protein-modulated microbiota, results in a compositional shift in the gut microbiota, characterized by an increased abundance of beneficial taxa such as Akkermansia, Lachnospiraceae NK4A136, and Parasutterella. Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Tuzzerella are known SCFA producers and mediate anti-inflammatory pathways (19). Akkermansia has been shown to maintain the mucus layer in the gut (38). These taxa have been associated with improved intestinal barrier function and reduced systemic inflammation. PICRUSt2-based functional inference suggested enrichment of microbial pathways related to amino acid degradation and fatty acid metabolism following Veg-FMT. These predictions were accompanied by measurable changes in microbial associated metabolites, including increased caproic acid, providing observational support for altered microbial metabolic potential. (39,40).

Changes in the gut microbiota can influence liver function. Our proteomics and pathway analyses revealed that Veg-FMT significantly activated PPARα signaling, a key regulator of impaired fatty acid oxidation in ALD (41). The upregulation of PPARα and its targets (Cpt1, Acox1, and Fabp1) enhanced mitochondrial and peroxisomal β-oxidation, reducing hepatic lipid accumulation. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARα attenuated the protective metabolic effects of Veg-FMT, supporting a functional role for PPARα signaling in these responses.. These results align with those of previous studies highlighting PPARα as a therapeutic target in ALD (42,43).

Microbial mediators derived from dietary protein fermentation may modulate PPARα signaling. In the colon, microbial fermentation of dietary proteins generates SCFAs and other metabolites (39). Among these metabolites, caproic acid, a six-carbon fatty acid, emerged from our metabolomic analysis as a candidate mediator of PPARα-associated metabolic responses. Fatty acids can interact directly with PPARα and modulate its activity (44). Consistently, previous studies have shown that short- and medium-chain fatty acids contribute to cellular energy metabolism and can influence lipid metabolic pathways (24). In vitro and in vivo supplementation with caproic acid reduced hepatic lipid accumulation and altered fatty acid utilization, while these effects were attenuated by PPARα inhibition. Consistent with the established ability of fatty acids to interact with PPARα, BLI analysis demonstrated direct interaction between caproic acid and the PPARα ligand-binding domain, providing complementary biophysical evidence for PPARα engagement by caproic acid. Together, these findings support a role for caproic acid in PPARα-dependent hepatic metabolic responses. Notably, caproic acid-mediated improvement in hepatic lipid homeostasis was also associated with reduced triglyceride accumulation and downregulation of the lipid droplet-associated protein PLIN2, whereas lipid export genes (ApoB and MTP) were only modestly or non-significantly altered, indicating that steatosis attenuation was driven primarily by reduced lipid storage and enhanced fatty acid β-oxidation rather than increased VLDL export (45,46).

However, the study has several limitations. Findings are based on an animal model and require validation in human studies for FMT application. The long-term safety and broader metabolic impacts of Veg-FMT remain unknown. The modest sample size and inter-individual variability across omics analyses may limit statistical power and increase the risk of false-positive associations; therefore, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Furthermore, individual microbiota variability could influence treatment reproducibility, highlighting the need for personalized approaches in future research. The one-week post-FMT observation period was designed to capture early therapeutic and mechanistic responses but is insufficient to establish durable fibrosis reversal or long-term structural remodeling; longer-term studies are needed to determine the persistence of these effects. Short-course FMT has shown beneficial outcomes in patients with ALD, including a seven-day FMT course in severe alcoholic hepatitis (8,47) and a single FMT session in alcohol-associated ACLF (48), with a meta-analysis supporting improved short-term survival (49). However, although we observed a rapid reduction in fibrosis after FMT in this animal model, the response is likely to be slower in patients. In clinical studies, liver stiffness changed over one week to one month in alcohol-associated cirrhosis without a change in fibrosis grade (50). Fibrosis improvement in patients may therefore take weeks to months. Given the role of PPARα in ALD, pharmacological activation of this pathway could be explored as a therapeutic strategy. Elafibranor, a dual PPARα/δ agonist, has shown promise in improving liver function and reducing inflammation in ALD (51).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of Veg-FMT. We show that preconditioning the donor microbiota with a plant-protein diet is key to enhancing FMT efficacy by promoting SCFA-producing bacteria and elevating caproic acid levels. Caproic acid, in turn, activates PPARα, increasing β-oxidation, suppressing lipogenesis, and improving hepatic injury and metabolic health. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of the specific pathways that mediate the benefits of FMT.

sec.title: Adaptation of mice to high-protein diets
sec.p: Male C57BL/6 N mice (strain code-632) aged 6-8 weeks and weighing 20-25 g were procured from the Center for Comparative Medicine, ILBS, Delhi. The animals were housed under barrier housing conditions following specific pathogen-free animal husbandry practices. The ambient temperature and humidity were maintained at 21–25°C and 50–70%, respectively. The Institutional Animal Ethics Committee approved the animal protocols, and the experiments were performed following the ARRIVE (Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments) guidelines 2.0. The animal experiments were performed in the Experimental Animal Facility of ILBS, Delhi, during the light cycle. Autoclaved corn cob bedding material and a ventilated cage system were used for the housing. A piece of M-block wood (Kansara Scientific, India) was supplied to the mice so that they could gnaw on it to reduce stress.

The animals were acclimatized to a liquid diet for 1 week. Mice were then fed incremental alcohol in Lieber-DeCarli liquid diet (Cat#F1258SP, Bio-Serv, USA) with thioacetamide for 12 weeks to develop the ALD model as described earlier (52). Control mice were pair-fed a non-alcoholic isocaloric Lieber-DeCarli liquid diet (Cat#F1259SP, Bio-Serv, USA; calories equated with maltodextrin). For FMT the donor mice were randomly divided into three groups: control diet donor, high vegetable protein diet donor (crushed soya chunks; RSI Ltd., India), and egg protein diet donor (albumin egg flakes; Cat#GLR09.020738). All the diets were kept isocaloric (Additional file 1, S.Fig 1A). Respective diets were given for 14 days, and their fecal matter was collected at day 14. FMT recipients were fed standard liquid diet for seven days prior to FMT. The measurement of body weight was conducted every week for each animal, whereas food intake was assessed once every two days.

sec.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation
sec.p: For the FMT study, 6 mice were used per donor group (three donor groups: Cd, Vd and Ed). ALD was established in four groups of animals (n=8 each): Abstinence (Abst), standard FMT (Std-FMT), veg-protein FMT (Veg-FMT), and egg-protein FMT (Egg-FMT). The stool from animal donors fed high-protein or standard diets was collected and immediately processed for FMT. Fresh stool (300 mg) was resuspended in 3 ml of sterile, ice-cold 0.9% saline. Recipient ALD mice received gut washes with 200 µl of PEG-4000 (Cat#81240, Sigma Aldrich, USA). After four hours, 200 μl of the prepared fecal slurry was administered via oral gavage. Three doses of FMT were given every other day. The experiment was terminated 1 week after the last FMT dose was given.

sec.title: Tissue collection
sec.p: The stool was collected pre- and post-FMT. All other tissue samples were collected at the end of the experiments. Blood was obtained via retro-orbital sinuses just before euthanasia (Ketamine, 80-100mg/Kg + Xylazine, 8-10 mg/Kg). Tissue samples were weighed and divided into two groups – one set snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C till further processing. The second group for histopathology was fixed in 10% formalin.

sec.title: Biochemical tests
sec.p: To investigate the effect of FMT, serum was separated from the blood by centrifugation at 3,000xg for 10 minutes. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), bilirubin, and triglycerides were detected by an Olympus AU5400 automatic analyzer (Olympus Optical, Tokyo, Japan). Serum endotoxin levels were measured per manufacturer’s protocol using Pierce Chromogenic Endotoxin Quant Kit (#A39552, Thermofisher Scientific).

sec.title: Histopathology and immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Post-FMT histopathological features of liver and ileum were assessed in the formalin fixed tissue sections (4 μm thick) stained with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) to capture immune infiltrations, steatosis (Oil red O staining) and fibrosis (Masson’s trichrome staining). Immunohistochemical staining was performed to assess extent of fibrosis using antibodies against α-SMA (#MA5115467, Thermo Fischer, USA) on hepatic tissue. The sections were washed and incubated with an appropriate biotinylated secondary antibody and then with streptavidin-horseradish peroxidase complex (PolyExcel HRP/DAB Detection System Two Step Universal Kit, #PEH002, PathnSitu Biotechnologies, USA). Sections were then counterstained with hematoxylin (#S034, HiMedia). The sections were observed with the help of a light microscope (EVOSTM M5000, Thermofisher Scientific, USA) at a magnification of 10x, 20x and 40x.

body.p: The study provides valuable findings suggesting that modifying the donor's diet improves the effectiveness of fecal transplant therapies for liver disease. The reported results are of value, and the evidence supporting the overall conclusions is solid, although the causal inferences regarding the effects of microbiota composition, as well as caproic acid signaling on the phenotypes studied, is limited and needs further confirmation.
Summary:

The authors aimed to determine whether dietary conditioning of fecal microbiota donors can influence the therapeutic efficacy of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). Specifically, they tested whether donor diets enriched in vegetable or egg-derived proteins alter microbiota composition and function in ways that enhance recovery from alcohol-induced liver injury. Using a murine ALD model, the study integrates microbiome profiling, metabolomics, proteomics, and functional assays to identify mechanisms underlying improved outcomes. The authors propose that vegetable protein-conditioned microbiota promote beneficial microbial remodeling and increased production of caproic acid, which in turn activates hepatic PPARα signaling and enhances fatty acid β-oxidation, thereby reducing steatosis and inflammation.
Strengths:

The study is ambitious and methodologically comprehensive. The central idea, that donor diet can modulate FMT efficacy in ALD, is compelling and potentially impactful. It combines in vivo disease models, microbiome analysis (16S rRNA sequencing), metabolomics and proteomics, pharmacological inhibition experiments, and in vitro validation in hepatocytes. This multi-layered approach is a clear strength and allows the authors to explore the gut-liver axis. The comparison between different protein sources (vegetable vs egg) is very interesting and the PPARα inhibition experiments provide relatively strong functional support for the involvement of host metabolic signaling pathways in mediating the observed effects.
Weaknesses:

Despite the comprehensive scope of the manuscript, several aspects of the study limit the strength of its mechanistic conclusions. The causal attribution to caproic acid remains incomplete. While caproic acid is identified and functionally tested, there is no direct demonstration that it is necessary for the Veg-FMT phenotype in vivo. The metabolomics data suggest multiple candidate metabolites, but these are not systematically explored. The study identifies specific bacterial taxa and, separately, key metabolites, but does not establish a direct connection between microbial composition and metabolite production. The use of GW6471 supports involvement of PPARα but does not fully establish specificity, as off-target effects cannot be excluded. Finally, it is not fully clear whether effects are exclusively microbiota-driven or could partially reflect transfer of diet-derived metabolites.

The authors have satisfactorily addressed most of the weaknesses identified in my original assessment. The additional functional and correlation analyses, together with the more cautious interpretation of the mechanistic findings, have strengthened the manuscript. Although some limitations regarding causality and the potential contribution of soluble metabolites transferred during FMT remain, these are now more appropriately acknowledged and do not substantially compromise the main conclusions.

Overall, I consider the revised study a valuable contribution to the field, highlighting donor dietary conditioning as a potentially important factor in optimizing FMT efficacy. The work retains its scientific relevance and potential translational impact.
Likely impact of the work on the field, and the utility of the methods and data to the community:

The work addresses an important and underexplored question: how donor characteristics influence FMT efficacy. By introducing donor diet as a modifiable variable, the study has potential implications for optimizing microbiota-based therapies. The datasets (microbiome, metabolomics, and proteomics) may also be valuable to the community, as they provide a resource for exploring gut-liver metabolic interactions. The translational impact will, however, depend on validation in human systems and a clearer identification of causal mechanisms.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: While the proteomic and gene expression data suggest activation of pathways related to fatty acid β-oxidation, these measurements do not directly demonstrate increased metabolic flux. The use of the PPARα antagonist GW6471 provides important functional support for the involvement of this pathway; however, this approach primarily establishes pathway dependency rather than directly confirming enhanced β-oxidation activity. The role of caproic acid as a central mediator is plausible but not definitively established. Finally, the link between microbiota composition, metabolic function, and host signaling remains partly correlative.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful assessment. We agree that the GW6471 inhibition experiments primarily support pathway dependency rather than direct activation of PPARα by caproic acid, and we revised the manuscript accordingly to avoid overstating mechanistic conclusions.

To functionally assess alterations in fatty-acid utilization, we performed Seahorse Mito Fuel Flex assays, which demonstrated altered dependency on fatty-acid oxidation following caproic acid treatment. We have clarified in the revised manuscript that this assay provides functional evidence of altered substrate utilization/dependency rather than a direct quantitative measurement of intracellular β-oxidation flux. [Lines 305-306]

We further agree that the relationship between microbiota composition, caproic acid abundance, and host metabolic responses is associative. To strengthen this aspect, we performed an integrated Spearman correlation analysis using matched microbiome, metabolomic, and phenotypic measurements. Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002 were positively associated with caproic acid abundance (ρ = 0.713 and 0.678, respectively; FDR q < 0.05), while caproic acid was negatively associated with hepatic triglycerides (ρ = -0.797, q = 0.006), AST (ρ = -0.779, q = 0.008), bilirubin (ρ = -0.764, q = 0.009), IL-6 (ρ = -0.763, q = 0.009), and ALT (ρ = -0.615, q = 0.043). These findings provide additional associative support for a microbiota-caproic acid-host metabolic axis and supported the selection of caproic acid for subsequent functional validation. [Lines 270-278; Additional file 1, Table S10; Fig. S8]

Finally, we have moderated the mechanistic interpretation throughout the manuscript to distinguish pathway association/dependency from direct receptor activation and to explicitly acknowledge the correlative nature of the microbiota-metabolite-host relationships. [Lines 345, 346, 405-407]

disp-quote.p: (1) While the Methods section states that each recipient mouse group consisted of 16 animals, microbiome sequencing was performed on only 4 samples per group. This sample size is insufficient, and the high inter-individual variability observed reduces the statistical power and representativeness of the data. I recommend increasing the sequencing sample size or, at a minimum, explicitly acknowledging the risk of false positives due to the small sample size in the Discussion.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. We clarify that 6 biological samples per group, rather than 4, were included for the 16S rRNA gene sequencing. We have revised the Methods to explicitly state the number of biological replicates used for microbiome and other omics analyses. [Additional file 1, Lines 51-52, 72, 113]

We acknowledge that the modest sample size and inter-individual variability may limit statistical power and increase the risk of false-positive associations. This limitation has been added to the Discussion. [Lines 423-425]

disp-quote.p: (2) The layout of Figure 4 should be adjusted. Panel A should be enlarged for better visibility, while Panel B should be reduced in size to balance the figure composition.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We revised the layout of Figure 4 accordingly by enlarging Panel A for improved visibility and reducing the size of Panel B to achieve a more balanced figure composition.

disp-quote.p: (3) A rationale should be provided for the selection of egg white protein as the animal protein control. Does this adequately represent animal proteins in general? Could the results differ if casein or whey protein were used? The current choice limits the generalizability of the conclusions, and this limitation should be addressed.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Egg albumin was selected as the animal-derived protein source because of its well-characterized composition, high biological value, and prior use in our ALD dietary intervention studies (1). We have added this rationale to the Discussion. [Lines 380-382]

We agree that egg albumin represents only one animal protein source and that other proteins, such as casein or whey, may produce distinct microbial and metabolic responses. We have therefore acknowledged this limitation in the Discussion and clarified that our findings should not be generalized to animal proteins as a whole. [Lines 382-385]

disp-quote.p: (4) The ALD model was established over 12 weeks, yet the FMT intervention consisted of only 3 administrations with a 1-week observation period. In the context of such a severe liver injury model, a 1-week recovery period appears insufficient to observe genuine fibrosis reversal, which typically requires a longer timeframe. The authors should discuss whether short-term FMT can truly induce structural remodeling or if the observed effects are transient.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. We agree that the one-week post-FMT observation period is insufficient to establish durable fibrosis reversal or long-term structural remodeling in a chronic 12-week ALD model. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate early therapeutic and mechanistic responses following microbiota modulation, including changes in intestinal barrier integrity, inflammation, endotoxemia, and hepatic metabolic responses.

Short-course FMT has shown beneficial outcomes in ALD patients, including a 7-day FMT course in severe alcoholic hepatitis (2, 3) and a single FMT session in alcohol-associated ACLF (4). A meta-analysis supports improved short-term survival (5). Although we observed a rapid reduction in fibrosis after FMT in the animal model, the response is likely to be slower in patients. In clinical studies, liver stiffness changed over 1 week to 1 month in alcohol-associated cirrhosis without a change in fibrosis grade (6).
We have acknowledged in the Discussion that the durability of these effects cannot be determined from the current one-week follow-up and that longer-term studies are required. [Lines 425-434]

disp-quote.p: (5) The results rely heavily on PICRUSt2 for functional prediction. As prediction does not equate to factual validation, the authors should exercise caution in their wording within the Discussion. Alternatively, I recommend supplementing the study with shotgun metagenomic sequencing to verify the existence of these pathways rather than relying solely on predictive algorithms.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We agree that PICRUSt2 provides predictive functional inference rather than direct measurement of microbial metabolic activity. We have therefore revised the Results and Discussion to explicitly describe these findings as predicted microbial functional potential and have moderated the corresponding interpretation. [Lines 159-160]

We have also integrated the PICRUSt2 findings with our metabolomic data, where predicted alterations in fatty acid metabolism were accompanied by measurable changes in microbial metabolites, including increased caproic acid following Veg-FMT. These concordant findings provide observational support for the predicted metabolic alterations, while not constituting direct functional validation. [Lines 390-393]
We agree that shotgun metagenomic sequencing would provide a more direct assessment of microbial functional capacity and consider this an important direction for future studies.

disp-quote.p: (6) Although Egg-FMT was less effective than Veg-FMT, it performed better than the standard FMT or abstinence groups. Why is the effect of egg white protein intermediate? Is this due to rapid digestion resulting in insufficient substrate, or differences in metabolite production? A deeper comparative analysis of the Egg-FMT group is required, rather than treating it merely as a negative control.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. We agree that Egg-FMT showed an intermediate phenotype and should be considered an informative animal-protein comparator rather than a negative control. We have therefore expanded the comparative interpretation of the Egg-FMT group across the hepatic, PPARα-associated, and metabolomic findings. Egg-FMT produced partial improvements in hepatic metabolic parameters and PPARα-associated fatty acid metabolism, although these responses were consistently weaker than those observed with Veg-FMT. Notably, caproic acid abundance was also higher following Veg-FMT than Egg-FMT, providing a potential metabolic correlate of the differential response. [Lines 26-265]

We have further discussed that differences in protein digestibility and composition of substrates reaching the distal gut may contribute to distinct microbial and metabolite profiles between egg and vegetable protein. [Lines 372-378]

disp-quote.p: (7) “Relying solely on the ‘inhibitor blocking effect’ proves only that Caproic acid's function is dependent on the PPARα pathway, not that it directly acts on PPARα. To claim direct activation, the authors must demonstrate direct binding between Caproic acid and the PPARα protein (e.g., via SPR or MST assays). Alternatively, a luciferase reporter assay driven specifically by PPARα response elements (PPRE) should be conducted. If Caproic acid induces luminescence, it would confirm transcriptional activation of PPARα rather than mere downstream activation.”

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important and insightful suggestion. We agree that the PPARα inhibitor experiments primarily demonstrate that the metabolic effects of caproic acid are functionally dependent on PPARα signaling and, by themselves, do not establish direct interaction between caproic acid and PPARα.

To address this concern, we performed biolayer interferometry (BLI) using recombinant PPARα ligand-binding domain (PPARα-LBD) to directly assess the interaction between caproic acid and PPARα. Caproic acid showed a concentration-dependent binding response across 31.25-500 µM, with a saturable steady-state binding profile and an apparent KD of approximately 46 µM (Additional file 1, Fig. S10). These findings provide complementary biophysical evidence for a direct interaction between caproic acid and the PPARα ligand-binding domain.

We have incorporated these findings into the revised Results and Supplementary Methods (Additional file 1) and have revised the Discussion accordingly. We have also clarified the distinction between the evidence provided by the two approaches: BLI provides evidence of direct physical interaction between caproic acid and PPARα-LBD, whereas GW6471 experiments support the functional dependence of the observed metabolic effects on PPARα signaling. [Lines 307-315 and 409-413]

disp-quote.p: This manuscript investigates whether dietary conditioning of fecal microbiota donors influences the efficacy of FMT in alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). Using a murine model, the authors show that microbiota from donors fed a vegetable protein-enriched diet (Veg-FMT) improves liver injury, intestinal barrier integrity, and inflammation more effectively than standard or egg protein-enriched diet-shaped microbiota. The study is promising and potentially impactful, but key mechanistic claims need to be softened or further supported. With clearer interpretation and some additional analyses (or reframing), the manuscript could make a strong contribution.
Major comments:

(1) The causal role of caproic acid in mediating the effects of Veg-FMT is not fully established. While caproic acid was identified through metabolomics and functionally tested exogenously, the evidence remains largely associative. There is no direct demonstration that microbiota-derived caproic acid is necessary for the observed phenotype, nor that its in vivo levels are sufficient to explain the effects under physiological conditions. To strengthen this claim, the authors could correlate caproic acid levels with disease and metabolic outcomes at the individual sample level. If feasible, approaches such as depletion or inhibition would further support its role as a mediator. Alternatively, the authors may wish to temper their interpretation and refer to caproic acid as a candidate mediator rather than a definitive one.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We agree that the current findings do not establish that microbiota-derived caproic acid is necessary or sufficient to mediate the effects of Veg-FMT. We have therefore moderated our interpretation and refer to caproic acid as a candidate mediator rather as the definitive mediator.

We have now performed the biolayer interferometry (BLI) assay to directly assess the interaction between caproic acid and the PPARα ligand-binding domain, providing complementary biophysical evidence for the proposed molecular mechanism. [Lines 307-315 and Lines 409-413; Additional file 1, Fig. S10]

To strengthen the associative evidence, we performed an individual-level integrated Spearman correlation analysis using matched microbiome, metabolomic, and phenotypic measurements. Caproic acid abundance was positively associated with selected Veg-FMT-associated bacterial taxa and negatively associated with hepatic injury, inflammatory, and metabolic parameters, including ALT, AST, bilirubin, IL-6, and hepatic triglycerides (Additional file 1, Fig. S8; Table S10). [Lines 267-276]

Nevertheless, we acknowledge that these findings do not establish caproic acid as the sole modulator of hepatic phenotype with Veg-FMT. Accordingly, we have moderated the mechanistic interpretation throughout the revised manuscript and clarified that caproic acid represents a candidate microbial mediator contributing to the metabolic effects of Veg-FMT.

disp-quote.p: (2) The link between specific bacterial taxa and caproic acid production could be clarified. For example, correlation analyses between taxa abundance and metabolite levels, or discussion of known producers, would help connect microbiome composition to function.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. To clarify the relationship between specific bacterial taxa and caproic acid, we performed an individual-level Spearman correlation analysis using matched microbiome and metabolomic measurements. Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 and Coriobacteriaceae UCG-002 showed positive associations with caproic acid abundance (ρ = 0.713 and 0.678, respectively; FDR q < 0.05), providing additional associative evidence linking specific microbial taxa with caproic acid levels. [Additional file 1, Fig. S8; Table S10; Lines 267-276]

disp-quote.p: (3) Given the reliance on predictive functional profiling, the authors are encouraged to more explicitly acknowledge the limitations of this approach and, where possible, integrate the metabolomics data to support functional interpretations.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. We agree that PICRUSt2 provides predictive functional inference rather than direct measurement of microbial metabolic activity. We have therefore revised the Results and Discussion to explicitly describe the PICRUSt2 findings as predicted microbial metabolic potential and have moderated the corresponding interpretation. [Lines 171-173, 390-393]

disp-quote.p: (4) Clarification of the experimental design regarding donor conditioning would be helpful, particularly how potential transfer of diet-derived metabolites (independent of microbiota) was controlled for.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important consideration. The donor mice underwent dietary conditioning for 14 days, after which freshly collected fecal material was processed and administered to recipient mice. The FMT procedure did not include a separate metabolite-depletion step; therefore, we acknowledge that transfer of soluble donor-derived metabolites present in the fecal material cannot be completely excluded. Also this component has been addressed in a separate manuscript (7).

Nevertheless, the effects observed following FMT were accompanied by distinct microbiota compositional changes and corresponding metabolic alterations, and the subsequent caproic acid supplementation experiments provided independent functional evidence for the biological activity of this metabolite.

disp-quote.p: Minor comments:

Several sections of the manuscript would benefit from careful editing for clarity and consistency (e.g., phrasing of gene/protein expression results, formatting of fold changes and p-values, and correction of typographical errors).
(5) Some phrasing is slightly overstated. In several sections, consider replacing "demonstrate" for "suggest".

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have carefully revised the manuscript to moderate overstated statements and, where appropriate, replaced “demonstrate” with “suggest,” “indicate,” or “support” to ensure that the conclusions accurately reflect the evidence.

disp-quote.p: (6) Typographical/clarity issues: the sentence "also protein expression of Zo-1 significantly increased" needs rephrasing; inconsistent formatting (e.g., FC, spacing, punctuation).

body.p: We have carefully edited the manuscript for clarity and consistency, including rephrasing the sentence "also protein expression of Zo-1 significantly increased" [Lines 106-107] and standardizing the formatting.

disp-quote.p: (7) Ensure all supplementary references are consistent (some formatting irregularities).

body.p: We have carefully checked the references to ensure consistent formatting and numbering.

disp-quote.p: (8) Terminology: "protein-educated microbiota" is unusual. Consider simplifying.

body.p: We agree that the term “protein-educated microbiota” may be unclear. We have replaced it throughout the manuscript with “protein-conditioned microbiota” where appropriate to improve clarity and consistency.

disp-quote.p: The authors use the fact that the PPARα inhibitor blocked changes in FASN to argue that Caproic acid inhibits lipogenesis via PPARα. This logic seems flawed, because FASN is not directly regulated by PPARα. Therefore, the observed changes in FASN cannot be used as evidence for the proposed PPARα-mediated mechanism.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We agree that FASN is not a direct transcriptional target of PPARα and that changes in FASN expression alone do not demonstrate direct PPARα-mediated regulation. In our study, FASN, SREBP1c, and SCD1 were assessed as markers of the lipogenic response and were not intended to provide evidence of direct PPARα regulation. The role of PPARα was evaluated through GW6471-mediated inhibition of the overall metabolic response to caproic acid, together with changes in PPARα-associated fatty acid metabolism. Thus, changes in these lipogenic markers should be interpreted as part of the broader metabolic response to caproic acid rather than as evidence of direct PPARα-mediated regulation of FASN.
We have also revised the corresponding Figure 7 legend to use “attenuated” rather than “reversed” where appropriate. [Lines 763]
